extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy and aesthetics (art critics, poets, artists interested in theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and explanatory guidance for identifying and understanding 'genius' and aesthetic value: what makes perception, artistic production, and poetic/philosophical greatness. Emphasises objectivity/disinterestedness, perception vs will, imagination, reflectiveness, seriousness, and the universal in the particular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity / Disinterestedness of Perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic pleasure arises when perception is disinterested (free from relation to the will); objects are beautiful only as long as they do not concern us personally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty depends on 'pure objectivity, i.e. disinterestedness of their perception' — if an object were related to one's will (personal desire) the aesthetic charm would be abolished. Anti-pattern: perceiving objects as means to one's own ends destroys their beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity as Detached, Lofty Mood
rubrics_metrics.description: The sublime induces a lofty mood because the object moves along 'without any relation to us', participating in nothing and thereby allowing the will to vanish from consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the moon delights because it is 'an object of perception, but never of desire.' The sublime often includes shared perception with others, increasing unity and impression. Use when an object evokes exaltation through detachment rather than desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic Pleasure from Colour, Light, and Reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate unspeakable pleasure from colours, gleam of metal, transparency, sunsets, etc., ultimately depends on our interest being won for knowledge without excitement of the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These pleasures typically result from sensations 'perfectly free from pain or pleasure' and thus belong to pure knowing. Application: evaluate how sensory qualities draw the mind into pure contemplation rather than appetitive response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius as Predominant Capacity for Perceptive Knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is the predominating capacity for the kind of knowledge arising from perception (knowledge of the Platonic Ideas manifested in particulars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genius is contrasted with talent: while talent excels in discursive, calculative thought, genius achieves a profound, objective perception that yields original, universal insight. Works of genius typically originate directly from perception (painting, sculpture, poetry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeing the Universal in the Particular
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental characteristic of genius is 'always to see the universal in the particular' rather than apprehending particulars only as particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure of approach to genius: the degree to which a person perceives the universal (up to the most universal) in concrete particulars. Talent, by contrast, investigates particular relations; genius apprehends the essence or Platonic Idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination as Indispensable Tool of Genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination is required to complete, arrange, retain, and repeat perceptual materials and thereby enables genius to summon vivid images and truths at the right time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination lets genius 'call up spirits' that reveal truths otherwise weakly or rarely presented by naked reality. Anti-pattern: lacking imagination reduces one to gnawing at abstractions and limits achievement to calculative fields like mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of the Intellect from the Will (Instinctive Necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius consists in the intellect's emancipation from service to the will, allowing it to act freely and spontaneously; works of genius proceed not from intention or choice but from an instinctive necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moments of inspiration ('hour of initiation') are when the intellect, freed temporarily from the will, becomes a 'clear mirror of the world.' In contrast, intentional reflection is guided by will and cannot achieve the same purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflectiveness / Distinct Consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflectiveness — the capacity to detach and ask 'What is all this?' or 'How is it really fashioned?' — enables artists and philosophers to apprehend and express the objective world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflectiveness allows painters to repeat natural objects faithfully and poets to call up concrete presence via abstractions. It arises from an intellect freed from will and is the root of artistic and philosophical calling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness Directed to Objective Ends (Not Personal Welfare)
rubrics_metrics.description: True seriousness in art lies in pursuing objective, universal ends rather than personal, practical aims; good will (moral intention) is everything in morality but 'nothing' in art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persons whose seriousness is personal produce insipid or dishonest work aimed at flattering contemporaries. Genius sacrifices personal welfare to objective ends and is often unappreciated in its own time; greatness follows pursuit of the universal rather than self-interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality Rooted in Perceptive Knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The first manifestations of a surplus in knowledge show themselves in original, fundamental perceptive knowledge and its repetition in an image (e.g., painters, sculptors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genius produces original images directly from perception; talent produces works rooted in discursive thought and analysis. Evaluate originality by tracing work back to immediate perceptive insight rather than imitated mannerisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to Mannerism and Vulgarity (Avoiding Shells)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bunglers or merely talented imitators appropriate accidental externalities and mannerisms (the 'shell') instead of the kernel; this subordination of knowledge to will results in vulgarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: producing art to serve personal interests, social approval, or career advancement leads to superficial imitation rather than genuine creation. Genuine works avoid catering to contemporary humours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melancholy as a Frequent Accompaniment of Genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Melancholy commonly accompanies genius because a brighter intellect perceives more clearly the misery of the human condition; solitude from will's concerns fosters objectivity and a certain melancholy-serenity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and metaphors: Mont Blanc veiled in clouds with occasional uplifting glimpses; Goethe's remarks on poetic rapture arising from threatened evil. This is descriptive rather than prescriptive, but can be used as an indicator in psychological profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Perceptive (Pictorial) Knowledge Over Abstract Conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: All profound knowledge and the generative process of genuine art take place in pictures (perception); abstract conceptions yield works of mere talent or imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a work's insight stems from vivid perceptive imagery (primary) or from secondary abstractions and calculations. The latter indicates talent, not genius (except in fields like mathematics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of Intellect vs Will Balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is characterized by a reversed balance (more intellect than will) compared to the normal person (who is more will than intellect); this disproportion enables objective comprehension but also abnormality and disadvantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor: normal man two-thirds will/one-third intellect; genius two-thirds intellect/one-third will. Use as a heuristic for temperament and likely life outcomes (e.g., poor management of personal welfare).
